Relay does two things Jira never did for you: it fills your timesheet from what you actually did, and it shows you only what needs you. Everything else, Jira the way you'd want it, offline and from the keyboard, comes with them.

No timers. You work as you always do, and Relay proposes your timesheet from the evidence: the commits you made, the comments you wrote, the issues you moved. Each day is filled to your working hours, every draft says why it's there, and nothing reaches Jira until you accept it, one key for a whole month. Connect your repositories and your commits count too. In Settings › Repositories, Add a repository… and pick the folder where you cloned your code (how). Relay reads its git history on your computer, never changing it, and weighs each commit toward the issue it names. Without a repository, drafts come from your Jira activity alone. See how time tracking without timers works →

documents.t: Not every notification Jira sends. Every change in Jira, every issue's state and every workday is checked against your rules, on your computer. Only what a rule sends to your Inbox shows there: the mention waiting for your answer, the issue just assigned to you, the blocker that moved, the issue in progress with no update for three working days, the day you logged less than your hours. Everything else stays out of the way, kept in the issue's history, never in your list or your badge. Each item says why it's there, and you act on the issue right beside it: reply, move, assign, snooze, done. Rules can act for you, and ask first when they'd change Jira: the change waits in your Inbox until you approve it. Quiet when you want it: quiet hours hold notifications and deliver one summary, and a morning digest starts your day. The same answer every time: rules run locally, need no AI, and show what they'd do before you save them. See how Inbox and rules work →

documents.t: Relay is a desktop app for Jira Cloud. It keeps your issues on your computer, so everything opens at once and keeps working without a connection. Change issues without waiting. Move, assign, comment and log time; the change shows at once, is marked until Jira has it, and reaches Jira in the background. Everything can be undone with ⌘Z. See Offline and sync. Work anywhere. Fetch everything before a flight and keep working: reading, searching, editing, commenting, files, logging time. See Working offline. See your work your way. Lists or boards, grouped and filtered as you like, and an epic's progress, pace and timeline at a glance. See Lists, boards and filters and Epics. Keep notes and plans of your own. Draft issues live only on your computer, with comments and files, until you publish them. See Draft issues. Find anything. ⌘P goes to any issue, your recent ones first; tabs keep the ones you're on open. See Go to issue and Tabs. Do it from the keyboard. Every action is in ⌘K, every menu filters as you type, and most things have a shortcut. See Menus you can type in and Keyboard shortcuts. Ask the Assistant. It answers and drafts comments, release notes and summaries from an issue and its code, with a model you choose, and recipes make your own prompts one key away. Nothing reaches Jira until you post it. See The Assistant and Recipes.
documents.s: And Jira, the way you'd want it

documents.t: Download Relay for macOS, Windows or Linux from the releases page, then follow Getting started.

The Assistant is a chat beside your issues. It reads the issue, its comments and fields, its epic, and the code written for it in your repositories, and then answers a question or writes a draft: a comment, a description, testing instructions, release notes. You read the draft, change it if you like, and post it. Nothing reaches Jira until you press Post. It's optional. Until you choose a model, Relay doesn't show the Assistant at all, and everything else works the same.

Open Settings › Model and pick a Provider: OpenAI-compatible: any server with an OpenAI-compatible API, such as LM Studio, Ollama or llama.cpp on your computer, or a server elsewhere. Enter its Endpoint (usually ending in /v1), press Test, and pick the Model from the list. Claude: Anthropic's API, with your API key from console.anthropic.com. OpenAI: OpenAI's API (GPT and Codex models), with your API key from platform.openai.com. API keys are kept in your system's keychain and never shown again. A key for a server you run yourself is only sent over https, or to this computer. For a local model, use one that supports tool calls and has a context of 32k tokens or more: smaller models often ignore the tools, and a short context cuts long changes without saying so. What leaves this computer says where your data goes with the settings you chose. With a server on your computer: nothing. With Claude, OpenAI or a remote server: the issue you ask about and excerpts of its code go to them when you run the Assistant. Speed › Answer times shows how long the model took lately, once it has answered a few times, so you can compare models or settings.

In Settings › Repositories, Add a repository… and pick the folder of a local clone. The Assistant reads it and never changes it. With repositories linked, it finds the code for an issue by its key: a branch whose name holds the key (feature/NW-118-price-list-errors), compared with your main branch; otherwise, commits whose message mentions the key. It can then read more with its own read-only tools: list and read files, search, outline a file's functions, and look at commits and diffs. It never reads secrets or what you keep out of git: .env files, keys and certificates, credential files, anything under .ssh or .aws, files git ignores, binary files and very large ones. Nothing in a repository can make it run a program. With several repositories linked, it reads the ones whose branches or commits name the issue, and asks you which when it can't tell. Settings › Assistant › Use code from repositories turns code reading off altogether; answers then come from Jira only.

Open an issue and press ⌘J (Ctrl+J on Windows and Linux), or pick Assistant at the top of the side panel. A new chat offers your quick actions, the recipes you use most, as cards. Type a question and press ⌘↵. While it works you see each step (reading the branch, searching the code) and the answer as it's written; Esc stops it. Under the answer, a line says what it was based on: the branch, commits, files and comments it read. Open tool calls to see each one, what it was asked and what came back. Follow-up questions keep the conversation: the Assistant remembers what was said. In the box, / lists recipes, @ mentions a person and # brings in another issue.

When you ask for something to post, such as a reply or release notes, the answer is a draft, with its buttons under it: Post as comment (or Save as description, or Save to a field): sends it to Jira, like a comment you wrote, with undo. Edit: change the text first, then post. Copy, Regenerate (a new attempt) and Discard. Once posted, the chat says so, and the comment is on the issue. ⌘Z takes it back. A draft for the description or a field (Testing instructions, for example) waits in that field on the issue, marked Suggested by Assistant, with Accept, Edit first and Discard. The keys work on the draft shown: ⇧⌘↵ posts it, ⇧⌘E edits it, ⇧⌘⌫ discards it, and ⌥⌘R writes it again.

documents.t: ⌘6 opens the Assistant page: every chat in History, grouped by Issues, Epics, General, Rules and Scheduled, the open chat in the middle, and its Context on the right (the issue, its fields, and the branch and commits the chat used). ⇧⌘A moves a chat from beside an issue to this page, and back. ⇧⌘\ hides the history. ⌘N starts a chat that isn't about one issue: about your work, an epic (pick it with #), or anything you ask. These chats can look things up in Relay themselves: search issues, read your worklogs and activity, see Inbox. Recipes for your work in general start here, such as Standup notes or Weekly summary; see Recipes.

Settings › Assistant › Assistant can decides: Read (the default): it reads, and drafts. It can also make timesheet drafts, which stay in Relay until you accept them on the Timesheet. Read & write: it can also change issues, comment, log work and triage Inbox when you ask it to. With Ask before changes on (the default), each change waits in Inbox for your OK.

The Assistant runs in a process of its own. Its code tools read only the repositories you linked, never change them, and leave out secret and ignored files. With a model on your computer, nothing leaves it. With Claude, OpenAI or a remote server, what goes to them is what the chat needs: the issue, its comments and fields, its epic, excerpts of the code it read, and, in a general chat, what Relay's own lookups return. Rules can ask the Assistant for a draft, but nothing is ever posted for you: the draft waits in Inbox until you review it. More in Privacy and security.

A draft issue is an issue that lives only on your computer. It has a key of its own (D-1, D-2…), a page like any issue's, and nothing of it reaches Jira until you publish it. Nobody else sees it, it doesn't notify anyone, and it stays across restarts. These are drafts of issues. The dashed worklogs on the Timesheet are something else: see Drafts under Time tracking.
documents.s: Draft issues: notes and plans of your own

documents.t: Notes to yourself. In a meeting, someone mentions that the empty price list says the wrong thing. Save a draft, "Ask design about the empty price list copy", and get back to the meeting. It waits in My work, and nobody gets an email about a half-thought. Planning a feature. Before you share a plan, write it as drafts under its epic: "Price history for each product", "Bulk stock update from a CSV", "Spike: pick a currency rates provider". Give each a description, move them between statuses, link them ("D-2 is blocked by D-3"), and publish them when the plan is ready. Small things. A typo you noticed, a test that's flaky now and then, a log line that's too loud. Not worth a Jira issue yet, but worth not forgetting. Keep them as drafts, and discard the ones that turn out not to matter. When it becomes real, publish it: it goes to Jira as a new issue, with what you wrote on it.

Open New issue: ⌘N (Ctrl+N on Windows and Linux), the New issue button in My work's header, or the one on an epic's page, which puts the issue in that epic. In ⌘K it's New Issue…. Pick the project, the type and the epic, give it a title and, if you like, a description. Then: Save as draft (⇧⌘↵) keeps it on your computer as a draft. Create (⌘↵) sends it to Jira as a new issue. The draft opens on its own page.
My work: every draft, in a Drafts group of its own, first. An epic's page: its drafts, first, in a Drafts group of their own, whatever the filters or grouping.

A draft's page is any issue's page, and almost everything on it works: its title and description, rich text and all; its fields: status, assignee, priority, epic, labels and the rest; links to other issues, drafts included; comments, and files attached to it or to a comment. Each change is made at once and can be undone with ⌘Z, offline too. None of it goes to Jira, and none of it is counted in the title bar's waiting changes.

When a draft is ready, publish it: Publish in the draft's header; Publish draft in its right-click menu; Publish Draft in ⌘K, with the draft open or selected. Select several drafts in a list and it publishes each of them. What happens: The draft leaves Drafts and becomes a new issue on its way to Jira. Jira creates it with its title, type, epic, assignee and the other fields you set, all at once, so watchers see one "created". The rest follows, in the order you did it: changes to its description, its files, its comments, a move to another status. It takes its Jira key (NW-222, say). Its tab follows it to the new key, and, published from the draft's page, that page opens once Jira has it. If Jira refuses it (a field it requires, say), it stays your draft, on its page, and Relay says why: fix it and publish again. Publishing works offline too: the issue opens as a new issue, waits with your other changes and goes when you're back online, taking its Jira key then (Offline and sync). Publishing can't be undone with ⌘Z; while the new issue still waits for Jira, you can discard it from the list of waiting changes.

Discard a draft with the trash button in its header, Discard draft in its right-click menu, or Discard Draft in ⌘K. The draft goes, with its comments, files and links. Changed your mind? ⌘Z brings it back, with everything on it, and opens it again.

Both are made with the same form, and differ in when they go: A draft (Save as draft, key D-1) waits for you. It goes to Jira only when you publish it. A new issue (Create) goes to Jira straight away. Made offline, it shows New for its key until Jira has it and gives it a real one; it's already on its way, waiting with your other changes.
documents.s: A draft or a new issue?

documents.t: An AI app connected to Relay's MCP server can save drafts too, so it can suggest several issues from a conversation for you to read first. Making a draft needs no approval, since nothing leaves your computer; publishing one is a change to Jira, so it needs the server's read-write mode.

An epic's page answers "where is this at?" in one look: how much is done, what's in progress, who's on it, and whether it'll make its target. It's one click from the sidebar, and it works offline once Relay has read it.

The sidebar. Under Projects, each project you follow folds open to its open epics, and to the epics your own issues are in. The number beside an epic is how many of your open issues it holds. Click an epic to show its page. ⌘P. Type the epic's key or a word of its name, as for any issue (see Go to issue). From one of its issues. The epic in the issue's breadcrumb opens the epic's page. Projects and epics in the sidebar can be turned off in Settings › Appearance › Show projects and epics in the sidebar.

The top of the page says what the epic is and how far along: its title and summary (the first paragraph of its description); its status, its lead (the epic's assignee), its target (its due date) and how many issues it has; a progress bar split by status: done, in review, in progress, blocked and to do, with done's share as a percentage and each part's figure under it. When any of its issues has story points, the bar counts points; otherwise it counts issues. The head scrolls away as you go down the issues, and the breadcrumb stays.

Below the head are all of the epic's issues, not only yours. The switch at the end of the bar over them shows them as a list (⌥⌘L), a board (⌥⌘B) or a timeline (⌥⌘T). The page remembers which you chose. The list and the board work as on My work (see Lists, boards and filters): the same rows and cards, keys, selection and menus. Dragging a card to another column moves the issue to that status, the way Jira's workflow allows, and ⌘Z undoes it. On an epic's page, View › Grouping offers Status, Status Group and None: its issues already share their epic.
documents.s: Its issues: list, board or timeline

documents.t: The timeline puts the epic on a calendar, in weeks. Progress (the burn-up) draws two lines week by week: scope, the epic's issues by when they were created, and done, by when they were resolved. Today is a faint vertical line, and the target (the epic's due date) a dashed red one; past the target, the chart is hatched red. Hover over the chart to read any week's figures. At this pace says when the work would be done, from how fast issues were finished over the last 4 weeks, projected from today until it meets scope: for example "At this pace: 24 Nov (18 Nov – 2 Dec)". The range in brackets comes from the slowest and the fastest of those weeks, and is drawn as a faint band ahead of today. It gives a date only when at least 3 issues were done in those weeks; otherwise it says there's too little done lately, nothing done in the last 4 weeks, or All done. Hover over it to see what it's based on. Under the chart, each issue has a bar from its start date (else its sprint's start, else when it was created) to its due date (else its sprint's end, else when it was resolved, else today), coloured by its status. The rows follow the list's order and grouping, and select, open and take keys as the list's do. Zooming. Pinch on a trackpad, or ⌘-scroll, to zoom around the pointer; ⌥⌘= and ⌥⌘− zoom in and out, and ⌥⌘0 fits the whole timeline again. Zoomed in, scroll sideways (or ⇧-scroll) to move through the weeks.

The bar over the issues is the same filter bar as on My work, with one more pill: Assignee, for whose issues show. ⌘F chooses people: you first, then whoever has the most issues, and Unassigned last. ⌥M shows only yours. Filter (⇧⌘F) adds any other field: status, type, priority, links, due date and the rest. The list, the board and the timeline show what the filters let through; the progress bar and the head's figures stay the whole epic's. With people chosen, the pace reads At your pace (only you) or At their pace, since it counts only their issues. Each epic keeps its own filters, also after you quit Relay.

The right panel shows the Epic: its Releases (the fix versions of its issues, each with how many are done), its Details (Lead, Start, Target and Labels, which you can change in place), its Development and its Links. Select an issue in the list or board and the panel shows that issue, with Epic beside it in the panel's header to switch back. ⌥⌘1 shows the epic, ⌥⌘2 the selected issue.

New issue in the header creates an issue in the epic. To plan before anything reaches Jira, save it as a draft issue instead: drafts stay on your computer and come first on the epic's page, in a Drafts group of their own, whatever the filters, until you publish them.

Download the build for your computer from the releases page. macOS: unzip it and move Relay to Applications. Until Relay is signed with an Apple Developer ID, macOS asks before opening it the first time: open it from Finder with Control-click › Open. Windows: run the Setup file. Until the installer is signed, Windows may show "Windows protected your PC": choose More info › Run anyway. Linux: install the package for your distribution. Relay checks for new versions itself (Settings › General › Updates) and only installs a release signed by its publisher.

The first time Relay opens, it asks you to connect to Jira Cloud. Either: Sign in with your Atlassian account in the browser, and you come straight back to Relay; or Use an API token for your site, made on your Atlassian account's security page. Your sign-in is kept in your computer's keychain, never in Relay's files.

Right after connecting, Relay asks only for what it can't work out alone, and every step can be skipped: Projects: the projects Relay follows, for Triage and the sidebar. It starts with the projects of your own issues. Your commit email: so your commits count toward your timesheet's drafts (see Time tracking without timers), when git doesn't say who you are. Then Relay reads your issues in the background. My work, Inbox and the rest fill in as they arrive; you can start working at once.

One more thing worth a minute: in Settings › Repositories, click Add a repository… and pick the folder of each local clone you work in. Relay reads their git history on your computer, so your commits show on the Activity page and count toward your timesheet's drafts, each toward the issue it names. The Assistant can read their code too. Relay never changes a repository. See Your repositories for the details, and Time tracking without timers for what your commits become.

⌘K runs anything: every command, page and setting is in it. ⌘P goes to an issue: your recent ones first, and any you search for. See Go to issue. ⌘1 to ⌘8 show the pages in the sidebar's order. ⌘Z undoes the last change, wherever you made it. The full list is in Keyboard shortcuts.
⌘P (Ctrl+P on Windows and Linux) opens Go to issue: the quickest way to any issue, whether you opened it a minute ago or have never seen it.

With nothing typed, Go to issue lists: Recent: the issues you opened lately, newest first. One still open in a tab has a dot beside it. My work: your issues that aren't done yet and aren't already under Recent. So the issue you were just on is usually first: ⌘P, then ↵. With the Pinned or In tabs filter on (see Filters), it lists those issues instead, in the sidebar's order. Not done leaves out the done ones of whatever it lists. Jump by number. Type just a number, such as 2318, to go to that issue in the project you used last (NW-2318). The key bar shows which project that is.

Type to search. Relay searches the issues it keeps on your computer as you type, the key, summary, description and comments, and lists the best matches at once. A match found somewhere other than its summary says where on a second line (a comment, the description). Once you pause, Relay also asks Jira and adds what it finds that isn't already listed, under In Jira. So an issue you've never opened in Relay is found too. Under Look for, Relay offers to turn what you typed into a narrower search: the words only in comments, the description or the summary, or a person ("Comments by", "Anything by", "Assigned to", "Mentioning"). You can also type search operators, such as from:me, status:review or updated:>7d. They're the same as in ⌘K; see Search operators.

The filters sit under the search field. Click them, or press ⇥ to reach them: ← and → move between them, ↵ turns one on or off, ⌫ removes a person, and ↓ goes back to the results. Where the words are: Comments, Description or Summary. Who: By… (comments by someone), From… (anything by someone), Assignee… and Mentions…. Each asks for the person. Which issues: Not done, In tabs (open in a tab), and Pinned. With nothing typed, In tabs and Pinned list their issues at once; typing searches among them.

The key bar at the bottom shows the keys: ↵ opens the issue. ⌘T opens it in a tab in the background, so you can open several. ⌥⌘P pins it. ⌘↵ opens it in Jira, in your browser. These are the defaults; Keyboard shortcuts lists them all, and you can change them in Settings › Keyboard.

Inbox exists to hide what doesn't need you. Every change from Jira, every issue's state and every workday is checked against your rules, and only what a rule sends to Inbox shows in the list. Everything else is hidden: kept, and visible in the issue's activity, but never in the list or the badge. Relay comes with rules that cover the usual cases (mentions, assignments, reviews you're asked for). You can turn them off, change them, or add your own on the Rules page.

Open an item to see what changed, with the issue beside it. Mark it read, snooze it until later, or clear it when you're done. Act on the issue right there: move it, reply, assign it. Each change can be undone with ⌘Z.

A rule reads like a sentence: when something happens, if the issue is a certain way, then do something. When: a change arrives (a comment, a status change, a mention), an issue is in a certain state (in progress with no update for three working days), or a workday is a certain way (time not logged). If: conditions on the issue or the change: project, status, who did it, what field changed. Then: send it to Inbox, hide it, notify you, snooze it, ask the Assistant, or change the issue in Jira (move it, comment, set a field, add it to a release). A rule that changes Jira can ask you first: its change waits in Inbox until you approve it. Rules run on your computer, the same way every time, and need no model. Before you save a rule, its preview shows what it would have done with what's already stored.
Changed rules apply to what arrives from then on. To apply them to what's already stored, save with "Re-check" or run Re-check Inbox from ⌘K.
Every menu in Relay works the same way: a row's right-click menu, the menu of a field such as Status or Assignee, a page's View menu, a tab's menu in the sidebar. Open it, just type, and press ↵.

Right-click an issue row, a card, a tab in the sidebar or an Inbox item. ⇧F10 or the Menu key opens the same menu for the row under the cursor. Click a field: the chips under an issue's title, or a row of its Details. Press a field's key on the row under the cursor in My work, Inbox or an epic: ⌥S for status, ⌥A for assignee, ⌥P for priority. An issue's menu is the same everywhere you open it. Its fields come first, each a submenu: Status, Priority, Assignee, Epic, Sprint, Fix versions, Reporter and the rest. Then Open in tab, Open in browser, Peek, Copy key, Copy link and Ask the Assistant, and after them what belongs to the place you opened it from. Each row shows its shortcut beside it, so a menu also teaches you the keys.

Start typing while a menu is open. A search field appears with what you typed, and the rows become every match, both in this menu and in its submenus. A match from a submenu shows where it lives first, quieter: Status › In Review. A row matches when its name contains what you typed, anywhere in it and in any case: rev finds In Review. The first match is lit, so ↵ picks it. The search reaches two submenus deep. It doesn't go into Link to issue: open that one and type there. So to move an issue to In Review you don't need the Status submenu at all: right-click, type review, press ↵.

Key In a menu ↑ ↓ Move between rows. Home and End go to the first and last. ↵ Pick the lit row, or open its submenu. Space too, when not typing. → Open the lit row's submenu. ← Go back from a submenu. Esc Clear what you typed; then go back a level, or close the menu. ⇥ Close the whole menu. Pointing works too: resting the pointer on a row opens its submenu.

Assignee and Reporter have their search field from the start, so you type straight away. Before you type they list you (and Assignee's Unassigned), then the people Relay knows, most seen first. Typing finds anyone in Jira, not only the people listed.

Change an issue's status and assignee without touching the mouse: In My work, move to the issue with ↑ ↓. Press ⌥S, type rev, press ↵. The issue moves to In Review. Press ⌥A, type tom, press ↵. It's Tom Becker's now. Each change is a step you can undo with ⌘Z. On an issue's own page, ⌘K offers the same menus: Change status of NW-118…, Change assignee of NW-118…. The Status menu lists only the statuses Jira allows the issue to move to, grouped like the board's columns. Keyboard shortcuts lists every field's key.

Relay keeps your issues on your computer. Everything you open comes from there at once, and Relay refreshes it from Jira in the background. To get ready for a trip without a connection, see Working offline.

When you change an issue (move it, comment, log time), the change shows at once and waits in line to be sent. The title bar shows how many changes are on their way. Offline, they wait, in the order you made them, and go when you're back online. Every change can be undone with ⌘Z. A change not yet sent is simply taken back; one Jira already has is changed back in Jira.
documents.s: Changes reach Jira in the background

documents.t: The status at the top right is one of: Synced: everything you changed is in Jira. Syncing, with a count: changes are being sent now. Offline, with a count: changes wait until you're back online. Signed out of Jira, it reads the same, and the changes go once you sign in again. Not saved, in red, with a count: Jira refused a change. See When Jira refuses a change. Sync failed, with a count: Relay couldn't read something from Jira (an issue, your week on the Timesheet). Click it to see the list: each change with its issue, what changed and when, in the order they'll be sent. Click a change to open its issue; hover it to Discard it. Try now sends everything again without waiting. The same list is Changes Not in Jira… in ⌘K, and Send Changes to Jira Now does what Try now does.
documents.s: The title bar says where things stand

documents.t: A change that hasn't reached Jira is marked where it shows, with a small icon beside it: A grey arrow: the change waits to be sent. Hover it to see what: "Priority not in Jira yet". Nothing to do; it goes on its own. A red mark: Jira refused it. Hover it to see why: "Jira refused the priority:" and Jira's reason. You'll see the marks on: Issues in lists and on boards: beside a status or an assignee you changed. The issue itself: its title, the chips under it, its description, the fields in the right-hand panel and its links to other issues. Comments, before the time. Logged time: in the issue's Worklogs and on the Timesheet. Files you attach aren't marked on the issue; they wait in the title bar's list with your other changes.
documents.s: Marks on what isn't in Jira yet

documents.t: Sometimes Jira says no: a field the project doesn't allow, a move its workflow doesn't have, a permission you lack. The title bar then says a change was refused. Open it to see each one, marked Not saved, with what Jira said. You can try again or discard it; discarding puts the issue back as Jira has it. A refused comment or worklog with words in it also offers Copy text, so you keep what you wrote.

Before sending a field you edited, Relay checks it in Jira. If someone else changed it since, your change isn't sent: the list shows it as Not saved, and you choose Keep mine (send yours over theirs) or Keep theirs (drop yours).
If the connection drops after Jira took a change but before Relay heard back, Relay checks with Jira before sending it again, so nothing is made twice.

Sync failed lists what Relay couldn't read, with Jira's reason and when it last read it. Hover one for Try again, or Dismiss for something that no longer exists (an issue deleted in Jira): Relay stops asking until you refresh by hand or start Relay again. Retry Failed Syncs from Jira in ⌘K tries them all.

Relay refreshes what's shown on its own. ⌘R refreshes the current page now, and Refresh Everything in ⌘K reads everything again, for the times you want to be sure. Refresh issue … from Jira in ⌘K reads one issue again.

Plugins will let you build on Relay: add rules and actions, pages and views of your issues, commands with their own shortcuts, and logic that reads your data and reacts to changes. The plugin system is being built. This guide grows with it: first the ideas a plugin builds on, then how-tos (each a working example plugin you can run), then the reference of everything a plugin may call, made from Relay itself so it's always current. Start with Concepts: they're how Relay works today, and how plugins will work too.

Every feature in Relay works without its interface. A click, a shortcut, a menu item, a rule, an AI app through MCP, and later a plugin, all run the same thing the same way. The window is one client among others: it shows results and asks you to choose when something needs choosing. For a plugin, that means you can do anything Relay does, without drawing anything.

Every action is a command with a name, such as issue.move or inbox.markRead. Commands take plain parameters and return a result. Whatever triggers an action runs its command by name; nothing calls a feature directly. A command that needs a decision returns it rather than asking: moving an issue to a status whose screen needs fields returns what's missing, and the window opens a dialog for it.

Data is read through queries and changed through mutations, both by name. Queries read your stored data and return at once, offline too. Each says which topics it depends on, so it's read again when one of them changes. Mutations apply locally first, are recorded as one undo step, and queue the change for Jira. If Jira refuses, the change is marked and can be retried or discarded.

A store is live, app-wide state with a name (the connection, the sync status, your preferences). Any window or plugin can read it and watch it change; it changes only through commands. A topic names a piece of data ("this issue", "My work's list", "this week's worklogs"). When data changes, Relay announces its topics, and everything that depends on them refreshes.
Rules are data, checked by one engine that runs on your computer and always gives the same answer. Every rule can be run as a dry run first, which says what it would do and why, without doing it.

Your data lives on your computer, and Jira is synced in the background. Reads never wait for the network, and changes made offline reach Jira in order when you're back online. A plugin gets the same for free.

Relay keeps your issues in a database on your computer and talks to Jira directly: there's no Relay server in between. Your Jira sign-in and any model API keys are kept in your computer's keychain, never in Relay's files. Settings › Data shows how much is stored and lets you clear it.
documents.s: Your data stays on your computer

documents.t: To Jira: your reads and your changes, over HTTPS. To your model: only when you ask the Assistant something, and only to the model you chose (a local one, or Claude or OpenAI with your own key). To GitHub: a check for new versions, which you can turn off (Settings › General › Updates). Nothing else leaves your computer.

Anyone in your Jira site can write a description or a comment, so Relay treats what it shows as untrusted: Links open in your browser only when they're web or email links. Anything else (a file on your computer, a script, another app's link) never opens. A plain http link, a local address or a look-alike domain asks first and shows where it really goes. Images and files are shown only when they're what they say they are, and never run.

The Assistant reads an issue and, if you link one, a repository on your computer, read-only. It never reads secret files such as keys and .env files, and nothing it writes reaches Jira until you post it. The MCP server lets an AI app on your computer use your Jira data through Relay. It's off until you turn it on, only accepts apps on your computer that hold its token, and can't change anything unless you allow it. Turning access up (letting the Assistant or MCP apps change things, or no longer asking first) always asks you to confirm.
documents.s: The Assistant and the MCP server

documents.t: Relay installs an update only when it's signed with its publisher's key and every file matches what was signed.

A recipe is a job you give the Assistant again and again: what to ask, what it reads, and where the answer goes. Testing instructions reads the issue, its comments and its code, and writes instructions a tester can follow; Standup notes reads what you did yesterday and what's in progress, and writes your standup. Relay comes with a set, and you can change them or write your own. Recipes need the Assistant: they show once a model is set up.

On one issue: Recipe What it does Result Description from code Writes the issue's description from the code change: summary, changes, how to try it The description Release notes A release note for the people who use the product, from the issue and its change A comment draft Testing instructions Steps a tester who can't read code can follow, with what to expect, edge cases and open questions The issue's Testing instructions field, if it has one; else a comment draft What’s left in code? TODOs, parts of the issue the change doesn't cover yet, missing tests, whether it's merged An answer in the chat What changed since last test? What happened since the issue last went to testing, and which steps to run again An answer in the chat Steps to reproduce Numbered steps, with the expected and the actual result An answer in the chat Edge cases Up to ten unusual inputs or states to try, each with its expected result An answer in the chat Summary The issue in a few sentences, for someone who hasn't followed it An answer in the chat Release note, plain language A shorter release note, with no technical words A comment draft What’s blocking it? What it waits on, since when, and who could unblock it An answer in the chat Ready to ship? Yes, Not yet or Unclear, with what's done and what's missing An answer in the chat Why is this here? Why an item is in your Inbox, and whether you need to do anything An answer in the chat Draft a reply A short reply to the latest comment addressed to you, in your voice A comment draft Was it shipped? Yes, No or Unclear, from its status, fix versions and merged code An answer in the chat About your work in general: Recipe What it does Weekly summary What moved this week in your issues and epics, grouped by epic, and what needs attention next Standup notes Yesterday, Today and Blockers, from your activity, worklogs and commits What’s blocked? Your issues waiting on someone else, oldest first, with who or what they wait on Timesheet gaps Days this week with less than 6 hours logged, and the issues you touched those days Recipes that need code (Description from code, What’s left in code?) are offered only while a repository is linked.

On an issue, wherever you are: Its menu (right-click it, or ⇧F10): Ask the Assistant ▸ lists your quick actions, then More recipes ▸. ⌘K: with an issue selected, every recipe is there as "Testing instructions for NW-118". The chat: a new chat shows your quick actions as cards; in the box, / lists every recipe. The recipe runs in the issue's chat, and its answer arrives like any other: a draft to post, or an answer to read. Quick actions, the recipes one click away, are yours to pick: Settings › Assistant › Quick actions lists the issue recipes to tick and drag into order. In Inbox, an item's chat offers its own: Why is this here?, Summarise, Draft a reply and Was it shipped?. Recipes about your work in general start a chat on the Assistant page (⌘6, then ⌘N): pick one of the cards, or type /.

⌘5 opens the Recipes page: every recipe, filtered by All, Issue or General, in the order menus show them (drag to reorder). Pick one to change it in the editor on the right. ⌘N (or New recipe) starts one: Name and Icon: how it shows in menus, ⌘K and the chat. Runs on: One issue, or General (your work, an epic, a sprint; its answer is always a note in the chat). Instructions: what the Assistant is asked to do, in your own words (Markdown). Reads: The issue, Comments, Rich-text fields and Code. Needs code keeps it out of quick actions while no repository is linked. Result: a Comment draft, the Description, one of your site's rich-text fields, or a Note in the conversation. Whatever it is, nothing reaches Jira until you post or save it. Changes save as you type; ⌘Z steps back through them. ⌘D duplicates a recipe and ⌘⌫ deletes it. The Recipes menu at the top of the page imports and exports recipes as files (Import…, Export ▸ All Recipes… or This Recipe…), so you can share them with your team. A recipe Relay came with that you deleted stays deleted; Restore Default Recipes brings them all back as they shipped, and Start Clean… removes them, keeping your own.

A rule can run a recipe for you: add the Ask the Assistant action to it and pick the recipe. On a rule about changes or an issue's state, an issue recipe runs on each issue the rule matched; a general one looks at the Matched issues, My work, the Sprint or a JQL search. With When › Every … at …, it runs on a schedule. A rule that writes your standup notes every weekday at 9:15: When it's done, Inbox says so ("Standup notes ready", or "Release notes ready to review" for a draft), and opening the item opens the chat. The rule never posts anything: a draft waits for you there. Chats a scheduled rule starts are under Scheduled on the Assistant page. See Inbox and rules for how rules work.

An issue, or any chat's subject, can also go to an outside AI app instead of Relay's own Assistant: Claude Code, Claude, Codex / ChatGPT or ChatGPT (web). The app opens with a short prompt already written (the issue and, if you picked one, a recipe's job), and nothing is sent until you send it there. Apps that work in a folder, Claude Code and Codex, open in the issue's repository. An issue's menu: Open in ▸, then the app: the issue as it is, or with one of your recipes. ⇧⌘J opens the issue in your default app, set in Settings › MCP & integrations › Open in, where you also choose whether Claude Code opens in Claude Desktop or a terminal. In any Assistant chat, the ⌄ beside Ask sends what you write to an outside app instead; Ask then reads "Ask Claude Code", and recipes picked with / go there too. The prompt stays short because the app reads the issue itself, through Relay's MCP tools. Turn on Relay's MCP server in Settings › MCP & integrations › Local MCP server, and add the app under Clients once. If an app isn't installed, Relay copies the prompt for you to paste. The chat keeps a note of what went where, with Open again, Copy prompt and Show prompt. Open in works without a model set up.

This page is made from Relay itself, so it always matches the version it documents. Type these in ⌘K or ⌘P (Go to issue). Several together must all match.
Plain words match the key, summary, description and comments, stemmed (“locations” finds “location”); the last one also as a prefix while you type. "Quoted words" match in that order.
The words in a comment (stemmed). With from: or by:, one comment by that person holds them. Also written comment:, comments:. Try: comment:"refresh token", from:me comment:deploy.
The words in the description. Also written description:, desc:. Try: description:idempotency.
The words in the summary only. Also written summary:, title:. Try: summary:invoice -is:done.
A rich-text field, by any part of its name, holding the query’s plain words; any text when there are none. Try: field:"Testing instructions" devtools, field:release.
A name, any word of it (“pop” finds Ana Pop), or me.
Someone commented, logged work or changed something on it. The excerpt shows their newest comment, else what they did last (logged work, a change). Try: from:me, from:"Ana Pop" comment:review.
Someone commented on it; unlike from:, assigning, logging work or other changes don’t count. The excerpt shows their newest comment. Try: by:me, by:"Ana Pop" comment:review.
A comment or the description @mentions them. Try: mentions:me.
Assigned to them; none for unassigned. Try: assignee:me is:open, assignee:none.
Reported by them. Try: reporter:me.
Names and keys match from their start: status:in finds In progress.
Its status, by name. Try: status:"In progress".
Its project, by key. Try: project:PAY.
Its issue type. Try: type:bug is:open.
Its priority. Try: priority:high.
One of its labels. Also written label:, labels:. Try: label:backend.
One of its components. Try: component:api.
One of its fix versions. Also written version:, fix:. Try: version:2.4.
In an epic, by its key or words of its title. Try: epic:PAY-776, epic:supplier.
A subtask of that issue, or in that epic. Try: parent:PAY-12.

open (not done), done, todo, inprogress (by status category), mine (assigned to you), unassigned, watching. May be shortened: is:prog. Values: open, done, todo, inprogress, mine, unassigned, watching. Try: is:open, -is:done, is:watching.

attachment, comment, description, assignee, epic, parent, label, due, link, subtask, worklog. May be shortened: has:att. Values: attachment, comment, description, assignee, epic, parent, label, due, link, subtask, worklog. Try: has:attachment, is:open -has:comment.
7d since 7 days ago, <7d before then, 2026-10-21 or today that day, 2026-10 that month, +7d ahead. Units: h, d, w, m (months), y. Also >= and <=.
When it last changed in Jira. Try: updated:>7d, updated:<2026-01-01.
When it was created. Try: created:>30d, created:2026-10.
Its due date; issues without one never match. Try: due:<today is:open, due:<+7d.
When it was resolved. Try: resolved:>7d.
This page is made from Relay itself, so it always matches the version it documents. Open Settings with ⌘, (Ctrl+, on Windows and Linux), or find any of these in ⌘K by its name.

How Relay starts and behaves on your computer. Startup Open at login: Start in the background when you log in. Search from anywhere: Opens Go to issue over any app, while Relay runs: comments, operators and all. Open to: The screen you see first. Dock badge: What the number on the app icon counts. Region Week starts on: Used by the Timesheet and worklog totals. Time format Working hours: Gaps outside these hours are never suggested. Break: Taken within working hours; the rest is a working day, the Timesheet’s target and the rules’ working day. Working days: The days of the week you work. Days off Days off: Holidays and leave: not working days. Calendar feed: Your calendar’s private iCal address (Google: Secret address in iCal format; Outlook: a published calendar’s ICS link). Days it shows you out of office are days off. Out of office: Read hourly and when you Refresh. Updates Check for updates automatically: At startup and every few hours, from GitHub. Nothing downloads until you ask. Version

Theme, density and what the sidebar shows. Theme Theme Colour: Selection, primary buttons and highlights, as picked: light colours take dark text. With tinted surfaces, the hue everything leans to. Surfaces: Neutral greys, a warm cream, or tinted: surfaces, statuses and labels leaning to the colour. Clay: Soft raised surfaces and sunken fields instead of lines, rounder corners and pills. Interface Density: Compact fits more rows on screen. Font size Show projects and epics in the sidebar Show counts in the sidebar Group tabs by epic: A new tab joins its epic’s group. Tabs you move yourself stay where you put them. Open issues in preview: An opened issue shows without a tab, and the next one takes its place. Open in tab keeps it.

When the app is allowed to interrupt you. What counts as worth it is decided by your rules. Desktop Notify for: Inbox items: whatever reaches Inbox, and rules with a Notify action. Sound Quiet hours: Notifications wait, then arrive as one summary. Morning digest: One summary instead of overnight pings. Rules Notification rules: What reaches Inbox and what notifies lives on the Rules page.
Click a shortcut to record a new one. Show key hints: The bar of keys under lists and boards. Shortcuts
Narrow issue searches in ⌘K, ⌘P and MCP with operators, like Gmail. Click an example to try it. Search operators: comment:, from:, field:, is:open, has:attachment, updated:>7d…

Your Atlassian connection and how often Jira is checked. Account Account Sync Sync every: Opening a page or the window still syncs what it shows. Sync when the computer wakes Keep history for: Done issues, activity, rule runs and unviewed images. Inbox items stay until you clear them. Last sync
The projects whose work Relay shows, besides your own issues. Triage lists their open issues nobody has. Followed Followed projects

Rule defaults, testing instructions and import/export. Rules Run rules after sync: Off: rules only run on schedule and on demand. Rules Testing instructions Field: Used by the Testing instructions condition. Template text: Instructions still equal to this count as not filled. Empty: learned from your issues.

How timesheet drafts share out a day from your activity. Drafts Worklog steps: Time logged or changed here rounds to the nearest step; so do timesheet drafts. Worklogs already in Jira keep theirs. Never draft time for: Projects or issues, comma-separated: SUPPORT is every SUPPORT issue, PAY-12 just that one. Ignore changes to: Fields, comma-separated, whose changes are no signal. Signal weights Commit: A commit of yours naming the issue. Comment: A comment you wrote. Status move: Each further move the same day counts half the one before. Created: An issue you created. Assigned to you: Fades like status moves. Hand-off: Assigning it to someone else; only alongside other work that day. Fades like status moves. Other field change: Fades like status moves.

Your local clones, for this account. Relay reads them and never changes them. Linked Repositories: Activity and timesheet drafts read your commits in them; the Assistant reads their code (with several, a chat about an issue reads the ones whose branches or commits name it, or asks which). Your commit emails: Comma-separated. Your commits are the ones by these or by the repository’s git user.email; git’s config stays as it is.

What the Assistant offers you by default. Everything here can be changed per chat. Quick actions Quick actions Code Use code from repositories: Lets answers and drafts read branches, commits and files linked to the issue. Changes Assistant can: Read & write lets it make timesheet drafts, change issues, comment, log work and triage Inbox, as an MCP client with write access can. Ask before changes: Its changes wait in Inbox for your OK. Timesheet drafts and triage run directly: drafts stay here until you accept them.

The assistant is optional. Everything else works without it. Assistant Provider: Claude or OpenAI (GPT, Codex) with your API key, or any server with an OpenAI-compatible API, on this computer or remote. Off turns the Assistant off. Connection Endpoint: The server’s OpenAI-compatible base URL, usually ending in /v1. Model API key Status What leaves this computer Speed Answer times: How long the model in use took to answer lately, whole turns: compare models or settings.

Let agents and other tools use Relay. MCP server Local MCP server: Agents like Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex and ChatGPT can read issues, triage Inbox and work with rules. Status Ask before write tools: Rule changes from MCP wait in Inbox for your OK. Triage runs directly. Allow Jira searches: Lets clients run JQL on Jira with your account, beyond the issues stored here. Port: Local only (127.0.0.1). Clients Clients: Each client gets its own token; remove one to cut it off. ChatGPT’s chats can’t reach a server on this computer; its desktop app uses Relay through Codex. Tools Tools: What clients may call. A tool ticked off isn’t listed to any client; Relay’s Assistant keeps all of them. Open in Default app: Where Open in…’s shortcut and the issue header’s button start a conversation. Claude Code opens in: Claude Desktop’s Code tab, or a terminal running the claude command.

Everything is stored on this computer. Storage Local database Cache attachments: Keeps images and videos you view for offline viewing. Other files open in Jira. Attachment cache limit: The least recently viewed go first. Cached attachments Clear data: Pick what to clear: copies of Jira data download again; your own data is gone. Reset Reset all settings: Keeps your Jira connection and rules. Sign out and remove all data
Relay Version Logs: For bug reports. Release notes: What changed in this version. Report an issue: A bug or an idea, on GitHub. Licenses: The open-source software Relay is built with.
An issue you open gets a tab: it stays in the sidebar, under Open, until you close it. So the handful of issues you're working on are always one click away, and they're still there tomorrow.
documents.s: Tabs: keep your active issues open

documents.t: Double-click a row in My work or an epic, or press ↵ on it. In ⌘P, press ↵ on an issue. ⌘T opens it in a tab in the background, so you can open several and stay in ⌘P. Open in tab in any issue's menu. ⌘T opens the issue you're looking at in a list's panel (a single click in My work shows it there, without a tab). Opening an issue that already has a tab switches to it.
documents.s: Opening an issue in a tab

documents.t: The sidebar's Open section lists your tabs, with how many there are. Grouped by epic. A new tab joins its epic's group, made when needed with the epic's name and colour. Issues without an epic sit on their own. You can turn this off with Group tabs by epic in Settings › Appearance, in a group's menu, or in ⌘K. Folding. Click a group's row to fold it, and again to unfold it. Click Open or Pinned to fold the whole section. Your own groups. Right-click a tab for Add to new group or Add to "…" an existing one, and Remove from group. Or drag a tab: onto the middle of another tab to put them together, beside a tab to move it, onto Open to take it out of its group. A tab you place yourself stays where you put it. A group's menu (right-click its row) has Rename and colour…, New tab in group… (⌘P, opening into this group), Collapse group, Open all links in browser, Ungroup (its tabs stay open) and Close group (its tabs close).

Click a tab in the sidebar. ⇧⌘] and ⇧⌘[ go to the next and previous tab, pinned ones first, round from the last to the first. ⌘P lists your recent issues first: a dot marks one open in a tab, a star one that's pinned. ⌘[ and ⌘] go back and forward through the pages you've visited, tabs included.

⌥⌘W closes the tab you're looking at. (⌘W closes the window, as in any Mac app.) The × on a tab's row, when you point at it. A tab's menu: Close, Close other tabs, Close all tabs. Close all, beside the Open heading. Close other tabs and Close all leave your pinned tabs open. Closing the tab you're on takes you back to the page you were on before it. Closed one by mistake? Press ⌘Z. Closing is a step you can undo, like the toast says ("Closed NW-118 · Undo"), and the tab comes back where it was. The same goes for opening a tab, pinning, grouping and moving: each is an undo step. Folding a group isn't. Typing in a tab's menu finds its entries, as in any menu: close lists all three.

Pin the issues you always come back to: a recurring task, the release checklist, your epic. A pinned issue moves to the Pinned section at the top of the sidebar, above Open, and stays there: Close other tabs and Close all leave it open. It leaves its group while pinned. Unpinned, it goes back to the end of Open. To pin or unpin: the star in the issue's header (Pin / Unpin); ⌥⌘P on the issue you're looking at, or on the issue lit in ⌘P; Pin in a tab's menu; drag a tab onto Pinned. Pinning an issue that has no tab opens one. Find a pinned issue. In ⌘P, turn on the Pinned filter (or In tabs for every open tab): it lists those issues at once, in the sidebar's order, instead of Recent and My work. Type to search among them only.

If you open many issues just to glance at them, turn on Open issues in preview in Settings › Appearance (it's off by default). Then an opened issue shows without a tab, and the next one you open takes its place, as in a code editor's preview. To keep the one you're looking at, click Open in tab in its header or press ⌘T. Pinning it keeps it too, and ⌥⌘W closes it. A preview isn't in the sidebar and isn't an undo step. Turning the setting off turns the preview into a tab.

Your tabs, their groups, your pins and your recent issues (the last 50) are kept on your computer. Quit and come back, and they're all there. With Open to: Where you left off (Settings › General, the default), Relay also opens on the page you were on, with Back and Forward as you left them. The undo history isn't kept: after a restart, ⌘Z starts fresh.

You never start a timer. You work as you always do, in Jira and in your code, and Relay fills your timesheet from what you did: the commits you made, the comments you wrote, the issues you moved, opened and picked up. It proposes the day as drafts, each saying why it's there. You look them over and accept them with one key. Only then does anything reach Jira. Connect your repositories first Your commits are the strongest evidence of your work, and Relay can only count them once it knows where your code is. In Settings › Repositories, click Add a repository… and pick the folder of a local clone (add as many as you work in). Relay then reads their git history on your computer, for the last three months, and the Activity page and your drafts include every commit of yours. It never changes a repository. See Your repositories. Without one, drafts still work, from your Jira activity alone. See Setting it up.

Nothing to remember. No timer left running over lunch, none forgotten in the morning, no Friday afternoon trying to recall Tuesday. Evidence, not guesses. Every draft comes from signals you can see: this commit, that comment, this move from To Do to In Progress. A draft says why it's there, and how sure it is. Your day, your hours. Drafts fill each working day to your working hours, less what you already logged, and skip days off, weekends and vacations. You decide. Drafts stay on your computer until you accept them. Change one, discard one, or accept a whole month in one go, and undo any of it. On your computer. Your commits are read from your own repositories, locally. Nothing about them is sent anywhere.

Signals. Relay keeps what you did, from Jira and from the git history of the repositories you connect, by time and by issue. See it on the Activity page. → Signals Drafts. ⇧⌘G turns a month of signals into drafts: each working day shared out between the issues you worked on, by what the signals weigh. → Drafts Review. Each draft says why it's there, down to the commit. Accept it, change its issue or time, or discard it. → Reviewing and accepting Logged. Accepted drafts become worklogs in Jira, like any time you log, offline too. Getting the most from it takes a minute of setup: your working hours, your days off, and the repositories you commit to. → Setting it up
A draft is a worklog Relay proposes: an issue, a day, a start and a length. It's drawn dashed on the Timesheet, beside the time you've logged, and stays on your computer until you accept it.

⇧⌘G makes drafts for this month. On the Timesheet, Drafts › Generate Drafts makes them for what it shows: the day, the week or the month. In ⌘K: Generate Drafts: This Month or Last Month. Making drafts again replaces that range's drafts with fresh ones, and can be undone with ⌘Z.

For each working day, Relay: Takes your hours: your working hours, less the break, less what you already logged that day. Shares them out between the issues you worked on, by what their signals weigh. Rounds to your worklog step (15 minutes by default), with at least 30 minutes per issue; the smallest fold into the larger ones. Stacks them from the start of your working day, in the order you first touched each issue. Days off, vacations from your calendar and days you don't work are skipped. A working day with no signals at all carries over the latest earlier day whose issues are still yours and not done, and says so.

Select a draft and Relay says why, over its issue: Drafted because: 1 commit, 1 comment, 1 status move. Signals opens the evidence: the draft, its day and its length, and how sure Relay is: Strong when your commits and Jira both point at it, Medium for several signals, Weak for one; when the signals came, half hour by half hour, for Jira and each repository, and the span you were active; each signal itself: the commit, the comment, the move. If the evidence is wrong, Not right? Change the issue or day… opens the draft to correct it.

Relay remembers what each set of drafts was made from. When you've done more since, or logged time on those days, the Timesheet says so (for example, "2 new signals and logged time changed on 1 day since these drafts were made") with Regenerate beside it.
documents.s: When drafts go out of date

documents.t: Drafts are yours to check. Nothing reaches Jira until you accept it, and everything can be undone.

Click a draft, or move to it with the arrow keys, and its issue shows beside the calendar with why it's there. Accept (⌥A) logs it. Edit… (↵, or double-click) opens it in the Log time dialog: change the issue, the time or the start, then accept it as changed. Discard (⌫) drops it. Select several drafts and the same keys act on all of them. A draft's menu (right-click) has the same, and the day's.

When the drafts look right, accept them together: Accept All (⌥⇧A) logs every draft the Timesheet shows: the day, the week or the month. Discard All (⇧⌫) drops them. Both are beside the drafts' line in the panel (8 drafts · 16h → 24h of 40h if accepted), in the Drafts menu, and in ⌘K.

An accepted draft becomes a worklog: it's drawn as logged time at once, and goes to Jira in the background like any change, so it works offline too. Accepting a set is one step: ⌘Z takes them all back, and they're drafts again.
Drafts are only as good as what Relay knows about your days. A minute here makes them right from the first month.

In Settings › General: Working hours and the break inside them: a day's hours are what drafts fill. Working days: the days drafts are made for. Days off, and a calendar feed: a private calendar link (iCal) whose out-of-office days count as days off. Days off show on the Timesheet, named, and get no drafts.

Your commits are the strongest signal there is, so this is the step that matters most. In Settings › Repositories, click Add a repository… and pick the folder of a local clone. Add every repository you work in. If git doesn't know who you are there (no user.email), add your commit emails, comma-separated. Relay asks for one when you first connect, if it needs it. Relay reads each repository's git history on your computer: every local branch, the last three months, again in the background while you look at the Activity page. A commit counts when its author email is yours, toward the issue its message or branch names. Relay never fetches, pushes or changes anything in a repository.

In Settings › Timesheet: Worklog steps: drafts round to this (15 minutes by default). Never draft time for: projects (SUPPORT) or issues (PAY-12) that should never get drafts. Ignore changes to: fields whose changes aren't work (Rank, Sprint by default). Signal weights: how much a commit, a comment, a status move and the rest count. See Signals. Left-out projects and fields still show on the Activity page; they just make no time.
A signal is one thing you did, at a time, usually on an issue. Drafts are made from signals, and nothing else: if Relay can't point to something you did, it doesn't propose time for it.

From Jira, your own activity on any issue: a comment you wrote a status you moved (To Do → In Progress) an issue you created an issue assigned to you, or one you handed to someone else a field you changed From your code: every commit of yours in the repositories you connect (Settings › Repositories › Add a repository…, see Setting it up). Relay reads their git history from your computer; it never pushes, fetches or changes anything. Which issue: the issue key in the commit message (NW-118 Handle bad currency codes), or else in the name of the branch the commit is on. Whose: commits whose author email is yours: git's user.email for that repository, or one of your commit emails in Settings › Repositories. Nothing is guessed from names. A commit that names no issue still shows on the Activity page, but makes no time.

The Activity page (⌘7) shows your signals: thirteen weeks at a glance, a square per day for Jira and for each repository, then the day you pick, half hour by half hour, and beside it every signal of that day, grouped by issue, the busiest first. Open a signal to go to it: a commit on its remote, a comment or a change on its issue.

Not every signal says the same about your time. By default: Signal Weight A commit 1 A comment 1 A status move 1 An issue created 1 Assigned to you 0.5 Another field changed 0.5 Handed to someone else 0.5, only alongside other work on the issue that day Repeats fade. On one day, each further status move, field change or assignment on an issue counts half the one before, so thirteen moves while grooming a board weigh about two, not thirteen. Commits and comments always count in full. You can change every weight, leave projects or issues out, and say which fields' changes aren't signals at all: see Setting it up.

The Timesheet (⌘3) shows your time: a day, a week or a month at a time. Logged time is solid, coloured by its epic; drafts are dashed beside it. The panel adds the time up by epic against your working hours, and says what accepting the drafts would make it.
Today (⌥T) comes back to now; ⌥← and ⌥→ step a day, week or month. Day (⌥D), Week (⌥W) and Month (⌥M) switch the view. View sets what the calendar shows.

You don't have to wait for drafts: log time on an issue from its page or from a row's menu. Like every change, it shows at once, reaches Jira in the background and can be undone with ⌘Z. Drafts made later count it, and fill only what's left of the day.

My work, Triage and a project's page are the same page over different issues, so they work the same way: a list or a board, the View menu, the filter bar, the keys and the right panel. An epic's page shares all of it too. My work (⌘2): the issues assigned to you. Triage (⌘8): new work in the projects you follow, unassigned and in no epic. An issue leaves it as soon as it's assigned or put in an epic. A project's page: click the project's row under Projects in the sidebar. It shows that project's Triage issues. Each view keeps its own layout, grouping, sorting and filters.

The list groups your issues by status, in workflow order: To Do, then In Progress, In Review and Done, each with its count. Each row shows the issue's status, type, key and summary, its epic, and when it last changed. A group folds with the arrow beside its name. On My work, draft issues you haven't published come first, in a Drafts group of their own. Click a row, or move to it with ↑ ↓, and the issue opens in the right panel: its status, assignee, priority and epic, its description, and its comments, activity and worklogs, where you can work on it without leaving the list.

The board shows the same issues as columns, one per status. Switch between them with the List | Board switch at the top right, or the keys: ⌥⌘L for the list, ⌥⌘B for the board. In ⌘K they're Show as List and Show as Board. Each view remembers which one you last used. Drag a card to another column to move the issue to that status, or press ⇧→ / ⇧← to move the card under the cursor one column. Relay moves it the way Jira's workflow allows: When the workflow leads to exactly one of the column's statuses, the issue moves there. When it leads to several, the status menu opens where you dropped the card, with just those, so you pick. When there's no way there from the issue's status, a message says so and nothing changes. While you drag, the columns the issue can't move to are dimmed. A move is saved on your computer first and sent to Jira, like any change, and ⌘Z undoes it. Cards drag only while the board is grouped by status or status group.

View, beside the switch, holds how the issues are shown. Each submenu names what's chosen. Grouping: Status (a group or column per Jira status), Status Group (To do, In progress, Blocked, In review and Done, each holding the statuses that belong to it), Epic, Parent, Project, or None. Triage starts grouped by project when its issues span several projects. Ordering: Updated, Created, Status or Key, then the direction in its own words (Newest First, Oldest First; Workflow Order; Lowest Key First). ⇧⌘O reverses it. Empty Status Columns: on, the board has a column for every status of your issues' projects, empty ones too, so you can drag a card to any of them. Off, only statuses with issues get a column. Columns: which of those empty columns show, one checkbox per status, and Show All. A status with issues always shows. Sync: Refresh (⌘R) reads the list from Jira again; Fetch Everything reads everything Relay keeps from Jira again (see Offline and sync). Reset returns this view to the defaults; Set as Default makes its options the default for every view without options of its own.

The bar under the header narrows the issues. Click Filter (⇧⌘F) to open the filter menu. Each field opens a submenu of its values, each with how many issues have it: Project, Status, Type, Priority and Reporter. Links: blocked by an open issue, blocks an open issue, has issue links, no issue links. Updated and Created: in the last day, 7 days or 30 days (Updated also offers "Not in 30 days"). Due: overdue, in the next 7 or 30 days, or no due date. Pull request: has one, or doesn't. Pick a value to add it; pick it again to take it away. Any clears that field. Type while the menu is open to find a value in any field. Combining filters. Several values in one field match any of them (Status: To Do or In Progress). Different fields must all match (Priority: High, and Type: Bug). Each filter shows as a pill, such as Priority: High: click it to change it, or its × to remove it. The count on the right says how many issues show, as in 2 of 8 issues, and Clear removes every filter at once. Filters are kept per view: My work, Triage, each project and each epic keep their own, also after you quit and reopen Relay. Each change is a step you can undo with ⌘Z.

Every issue list and board works the same way: ↑ ↓ move, and show the issue in the right panel. On a board, ← → move between columns. ↵ opens the issue in a tab; Space peeks at it in the right panel, opening the panel if it's hidden. ⌥X adds the issue under the cursor to the selection, or takes it out. ⌘A selects everything; Esc clears the selection. ⌥S, ⌥A and ⌥P change its status, assignee or priority; ⌥B links an issue that blocks it, ⌥L links another. ⌘↵ opens the selection in the browser; ⌘C copies its keys, ⇧⌘C its links. ⇧F10, or a right-click, opens the issue's menu. The key strip under the list shows these keys as you work. ⌘/ hides or shows it. Every key is listed in Keyboard shortcuts.
The right panel shows the issue selected in the list or board, and follows the selection. ⌥⌘\ hides or shows it, for example to see every column of a wide board.

When your Jira is connected to GitHub or Bitbucket, an issue's rail has a Development section: the branches, pull requests and commits that name the issue's key, and how their checks went. An open pull request shows its review (Approved, Changes requested, In review), a closed one how it closed. Click a row to open it in your browser. An epic's page shows it on each of its rows: the pull request's number beside the summary (#44). The filter bar's Pull request filter keeps only the issues that have one, or only those that don't. Like everything else, it's kept on your computer, so it shows offline too.
documents.s: Development: branches, pull requests and checks

documents.t: Relay keeps your issues on your computer, so it works the same on a plane as at your desk. What you change offline waits and reaches Jira when you're back (Offline and sync).

Without you asking, Relay keeps: Your lists: My work, Inbox and the issues your rules look at, refreshed in the background. Each issue you open: its description, comments, links and development. Your logged time, week by week, for the weeks you look at on the Timesheet. The images and videos you view, while Cache attachments is on (it is unless you turn it off). Lists bring each issue's status, assignee and other fields, but not its description or comments: those come when you open the issue. So an issue you've never opened has its row, but not its text.

Fetch Everything reads the rest at once, like downloading a map for offline use. Run it from ⌘K, or from My work's View menu › Sync › Fetch Everything. It reads, in turn: Epics: the issues of each epic in your sidebar. Issues: the description and every comment of each issue you're involved in, Inbox's and those epics'. Links: each issue's links and development (branches, commits, pull requests). Images: the image attachments on those issues, and a video's preview picture (not the video). Avatars: the pictures of the people on them. While it runs, the title bar reads Syncing. Click it to see how far along each step is, and Stop to end it after the request under way. What was read stays. If the connection goes while it runs, it stops and says where. What it couldn't read (an issue Jira won't give you) is listed under Sync failed in the title bar, and the rest goes on. Each step also runs on its own from ⌘K: Fetch Epics, Fetch Issues, Fetch Links, Fetch Images and Fetch Avatars. Images follow your attachment settings: with Cache attachments off, none are kept, and the cache's size limit still applies (see Where it's kept). Getting ready for a trip: Run Fetch Everything while you're online, and wait until the title bar says Synced. Look at the Timesheet weeks you'll need, so the time logged there is on your computer too. Open any issue you'll need that isn't yours or in your Inbox; opening it keeps it.

Reading: lists, boards, epics, issues with their descriptions and comments, the Timesheet and Activity. Finding: ⌘P and ⌘K search everything Relay keeps, search operators included. Changing issues: status, assignee, priority, fields, the description and links. A status can change offline when Relay knows where the issue can move, which it learns when you open the issue online. Comments and files: comment, reply, edit, and attach files. Time: log time, and change or delete what you logged. New issues: create them and publish them; they're sent when you're back. Undo: ⌘Z takes back any change not sent yet. Rules and Inbox: your rules run on your computer, on what Relay has.

Searching Jira itself: ⌘P's results from Jira, and looking up an issue by key that Relay doesn't have. A second status change on the same issue: Jira has to take the first before it says where the issue can go next. Choices Relay hasn't read yet, such as a project's sprints, versions or priorities: the menu says they load once you're online. Files Relay doesn't show: PDFs, documents and other files open in Jira, in your browser. Images you haven't viewed: an image in a description or comment that isn't kept shows as its name, saying it isn't available offline. Refreshing: ⌘R, Refresh Everything and Refresh issue … from Jira need a connection.

An issue's files are listed under its description, under Attachments, each as a tile with its name, size and age. Images show a picture; other files show an icon. Images in a description or comment show inline, where they were put. Opening. Click a tile. Images open in Relay's viewer, where you can zoom and move around, and videos play there. Other files open in Jira, in your browser. Right-click an image (PNG or JPEG) for Copy Image. Attaching to the issue. Any of: the paperclip in the issue's header, or ⇧⌘U; Attach a file to … in ⌘K; drop files on the issue. Adding to a comment. The paperclip in the comment box (⌥⌘U) puts a file in what you're writing: an image shows in the text, another file by its name. Pasting or dropping a file into the text does the same. The file is attached when you post the comment; take it out of the text before posting, and it never is. Removing. Right-click a tile and choose Remove file. ⌘Z brings it back while the removal still waits to be sent; once Jira has removed it, it's gone. Offline. Files you attach are kept on your computer and wait with your other changes; they upload when you're back online, before the comment that shows them. Until then, Relay shows them from your computer. Each file can be up to 100 MB.

Everything is in your account's folder on this computer. Settings › Data & privacy shows it: Local database: its size, and Show in Finder. Cache attachments: keeps the images and videos you view, for offline. Turning it off empties the cache. Attachment cache limit: 250 MB to 2 GB (500 MB at first). The files viewed longest ago go first. Cached attachments: how much is kept, and Clear older than 7 days, Clear over 5 MB or Clear all. Clear data: pick what to clear. Copies of Jira data (issues, descriptions and comments, images and avatars, worklogs) download again; what's only yours is gone for good. Changes waiting for Jira are never cleared. Settings › Account & sync › Keep history for also decides how long done issues, activity and images you haven't viewed are kept.
